http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27922.text: Big News Network.com Hungary faces "most critical 5 days" as drought threatens nuclear plant shutdown BUDAPEST, Aug. 2 (Xinhua) -- Hungary is entering its "most critical 5 days" as dropping water levels on the Danube River threaten the complete shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant amid an extreme heatwave, Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Sunday, warning that the plant could be shut down for more than a month. Speaking to local commercial television channel RTL, Magyar said the last remaining operating turbine at the 2,000 MW facility will likely be shut down late Sunday or on Monday. A complete halt to power generation at Paks, which accounts for nearly half of Hungary's domestic electricity generation,would mark the first full closure in the plant's 44-year history. Magyar explained earlier on social media that strict nuclear safety regulations mandate the shutdown because of record-low river levels needed for cooling water. He reassured the public that nuclear safety remains fully guaranteed, with around 50 water management experts assisting plant personnel to maintain cooling operations. The unprecedented energy crisis comes as Hungary braces for temperatures reaching 40 degrees Celsius or higher over these "most critical five days," placing immense strain on the national grid. The Hungarian government has introduced emergency measures to maintain grid stability. Under a decree that took effect on Saturday, mandatory consumption cutbacks can be enforced on major industrial consumers if necessary. However, Magyar noted that voluntary conservation efforts by businesses and the public have so far helped avoid enforced rationing. Major companies, including MOL, Audi, and Gedeon Richter, have pledged significant demand reductions. Nearly 300 companies have already pledged voluntary reductions for Monday, along with numerous state-owned firms, most local councils, civil society groups and churches, he said. To save power, decorative lighting on Budapest's iconic landmarks, including the Hungarian Parliament, Buda Castle, and the Chain Bridge, was turned off on Sunday evening. Additional measures include halting most rail freight transport between 5:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m. starting Monday, bringing reserve power units on standby, and maximizing electricity imports. "If Hungary can get through these most critical five days, temperatures are expected to drop by 5 to 7 degrees Celsius," Magyar said, adding that household restrictions remain an absolute last resort to maintain system stability. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: 0:44 CCTV from inside Riyadh airport shows moment of deadly airstrike – video Saudi Arabia Saudi Arabia further suspends flights after latest deadly Houthi attack on airport Energy minister says ‘fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon’ as paramilitary group again breaches stretched defences Why are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports and how are the missiles getting through? Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Mon 12 Oct 2026 07.49 EDT Last modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 09.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Saudi Arabia was forced to extend the suspension of all flights to and from its main international airport in Riyadh on Monday after a further round of Houthi missile attacks caused more damage and left one dead. The Gulf nation said it was taking the step after Houthi missiles killed 13 people on Saturday and left more than 300 injured. Saudi state TV broadcast CCTV footage that showed passengers deluged in smoke and falling masonry as they queued at the airport terminal to board a plane just as the Houthi missile struck. King Khalid international airport was being kept closed to complete verification of the airport’s safety, the Saudi aviation authority said. Saudi Arabia’s military spokesperson also said further missile and drone threats had been detected. View image in fullscreen Before and after the strike as people queue up for flights at King Khalid international airport on Saturday. Photograph: Saudi Ministry of Media/Reuters The closure came as the country pressed ahead with the 25th WPC Energy Conference in Riyadh, hoping to project an image of normality. The Saudi energy minister, Abdulaziz bin Salman, told the conference that “fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon”, emphasising that the resilience of the kingdom’s energy system and the determination of its people to confront crises. An urgent review is under way as to how Houthi missiles are repeatedly penetrating badly stretched Saudi air defences. Schoolchildren and some office workers were advised to work from home. The Houthis have also targeted the city of Khamis Mushait, and the King Fahd international airport in Dammam. Interceptor missiles are needed to protect government buildings, oil facilities and infrastructure hubs across a wide geographic area. The Houthis have vowed to attack Saudi airports across the country. Houthi attacks since last month have targeted fuel tanks at Riyadh airport and its affiliated warehouses, destroying a parked Airbus A320 passenger plane and damaging at least five other aircraft. The crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, has not been seen in public since Tuesday last week, reflecting the pressure he is under to find a way out from a war that has intermittently dogged his leadership since 2014. Inside Yemen , fighting continued in and around Taiz, the third city, and the most populous governorate, with Saudi planes mounting eight separate strikes on any assembly of Houthi forces. As many as 60 fighters died on Sunday from both sides. The governor of Taiz, Nabil Shamsan, on Sunday issued an urgent call to lift the Houthi siege and warned a shortage of medicines meant the city would soon run out of emergency surgical and intensive care services. Overall the Houthis claimed the Saudis had mounted 124 raids on Sunday. The Saudis are seeking to locate Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, with rumours of his assassination repeatedly circulating, but Saudi Arabia does not seem to have contemporary intelligence on his precise whereabouts either in the capital Sana’a or in its stronghold of Saada. View image in fullscreen A billboard displays an image of the Houthi leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, in Sana’a, Yemen on Sunday. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA On the diplomatic front, Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, spoke to the Saudi foreign minister, Faisal bin Farhan, on Sunday to see if there was a way in which Iran could act as a mediator between the Saudis and the Houthis, a group that Iran has trained and armed. A meeting of the UN security council in New York on Tuesday is expected to debate a resolution calling the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation. The exiled leader of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), Aidarous al-Zubaidi, called for southern forces to fight on all fronts, and not just to defend the borders of the former South Yemen, in a move that is likely to be welcomed by Saudi Arabia as it supports the week-old call by the UN-recognised government to drive the Houthis out of the whole of Yemen, rather than just from the southern governorates. The STC has a vision of an independent South Yemen that would recreate the separate state that existed between 1967 and 1990. The reunification of Yemen at the end of the cold war proved fragile and many southerners nurse longstanding grievances about the distribution of resources in the unified state. The Gulf has entered a new era of instability. If its leaders think they can rely on old alliances, they are wrong | Nesrine Malik Read more The STC’s authority has been challenged by Abd al-Rahman al-Mahrami, the Salafist leader who commands the powerful Southern Giants Brigades. Despite Araghchi’s efforts to reach out to the Saudis, Mohsen Rezaei, the more hardline secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, claimed Iran was hitting five or six small vessels in the strait of Hormuz every night, explaining the vessels were being used by the Emirati military to move oil through the strait to larger tankers, thus breaching the blockade that Iran is seeking to maintain to push up oil prices and weaken Donald Trump . Esmail Baghaei, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, said Trump’s treatment of Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including his call for the Ukrainian president to stand aside showed the risks in dealing with Trump. He said: “Being an enemy of America can be dangerous, but being a friend of America is deadly. The future is bright and tricolor™ About us Privacy Policy Terms of Service Ishkhan Saghatelyan lists Pashinyan’s major concessions Ishkhan Saghatelyan, a member of the Armenian National Assembly’s opposition Hayastan faction, has published a Facebook post titled “What Has Nikol Pashinyan Conceded?”, responding to a question raised by the prime minister from the parliamentary rostrum. He noted that he had previously presented the same list in the spring of 2025. “Today, speaking from the National Assembly rostrum, Nikol Pashinyan expressed surprise and asked what exactly he had conceded. I presented this list in March 2025. It is a non-exhaustive list of Pashinyan’s major concessions. He would do well to read it and remain silent before asking that question again. 1.Following Pashinyan’s orders (under what he himself described as a ‘verbal understanding’), Armenia’s armed forces withdrew from their positions in December 2020, leaving commanding strategic positions in Syunik under Azerbaijani control. This concession was subsequently justified by citing the threat of war. 2.On May 12, 2021, Azerbaijani armed forces entered Armenia’s sovereign territory without encountering resistance, first near Sev Lake in Syunik province and then in the areas of Verin Shorzha and Kut in Gegharkunik province, occupying approximately 41 square kilometers. Once again, you surrendered strategic positions without resistance, asking whether we really needed those snow-covered mountains. 3.In November 2021, a 21-kilometer section of the Goris-Kapan interstate highway and part of the village of Shurnukh were handed over to Azerbaijan. 4.On November 15, 2021, the Azerbaijani side established a checkpoint on a section of the Kapan-Chakaten road. The road was thereby surrendered to the enemy, cutting off the shortest and most convenient connection between six nearby villages and Kapan. 5.In March 2022, Azerbaijani units advanced approximately one kilometer into the administrative territory of Nerkin Hand without firing a shot and under peaceful conditions. They erected five tents there, establishing control over additional territory. 6.In April 2022, Pashinyan announced that Armenia would lower the bar regarding the Artsakh issue, fulfilling an Azerbaijani precondition under which Armenia abandoned its commitment to defending Artsakh’s right to self-determination. 7.On August 25, 2022, Berdzor, Aghavno and Sus were handed over to Azerbaijan. The transfer of the Lachin corridor, which connected Artsakh to Armenia, along with the surrounding settlements, was not envisaged under the trilateral statement of November 9, 2020. The transfer of these settlements also placed the gas pipeline and electricity transmission line supplying Artsakh under Azerbaijani control, with devastating consequences during the blockade of Artsakh. Moreover, these developments allowed the enemy to advance toward the village of Tegh in the Goris area, seizing the village’s agricultural land and pastures. 8.On September 13-14, 2022, Azerbaijani armed forces entered Armenia’s sovereign territory along the Gegharkunik, Syunik and Vayots Dzor directions, bringing the total occupied area to 220 square kilometers. We suffered more than 200 fatalities, primarily because strategic positions in those directions had previously been surrendered. 9.Through a verbal agreement in Prague in 2022, followed by a written agreement in Granada in 2023, Pashinyan fulfilled another Azerbaijani demand by recognizing Artsakh as part of Azerbaijan. In Granada, Pashinyan even signed a unilateral document recognizing Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity with a specified area of 86,600 square kilometers. In return, Aliyev has yet to recognize Armenia’s territorial integrity with clearly defined territory and borders. Azerbaijan subsequently cited these very statements when blocking the Lachin corridor and laying siege to Artsakh. 10. In September 2023, during the attack on Artsakh and the ethnic cleansing carried out there, Pashinyan fulfilled another Azerbaijani demand by leaving the Armenians of Artsakh on their own and publicly renouncing responsibility for ensuring the security of approximately 120,000 people who were Armenian citizens. 11. On February 28, 2024, the Armenian side returned Ruslan Penakhov, who had crossed the line of contact in the Tegh community area, to Azerbaijan as a gesture of goodwill, without securing the release of any prisoners in exchange. The same happened with Azerbaijanis who had entered Armenian territory in the Sisian area and killed an Armenian citizen in Kapan. They, too, were returned to Azerbaijan without an exchange. 12. In 2024, another unilateral concession was made under the threat of war, this time in Tavush, where Armenian troops withdrew from their positions, transferring the territories of four villages to Azerbaijani control. 13. At Azerbaijan’s demand, Pashinyan abandoned discussions in the negotiations concerning the protection of the rights of Artsakh Armenians and their return, declaring the Artsakh issue closed and thereby attempting to legitimize what Azerbaijan had carried out as genocide in Artsakh. 14. During the negotiations, Azerbaijan set a precondition requiring amendments to Armenia’s Constitution. Several months later, Pashinyan announced that Armenia needed a new Constitution and outlined specific deadlines for holding a referendum. 15. During the negotiations, Ilham Aliyev also demanded a joint application for the dissolution of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) Minsk Group. In a public post, Nikol Pashinyan agreed to meet that demand. 16. For a considerable period, Azerbaijani demands concerning the withdrawal of lawsuits from international courts and the non-deployment of forces along the border remained unresolved in the document under negotiation. In March 2025, Azerbaijan announced that Armenia had also agreed to these provisions. Thus, Azerbaijan’s condition concerning Armenia’s demilitarization was also partially fulfilled. 17. At Azerbaijan’s demand, a provision was included in the agreement with Armenia obliging the parties to take action against those operating within their respective countries ‘against the peace agenda’, thereby giving Azerbaijan an opportunity to interfere in Armenia’s internal affairs. 18. On June 12, July 3, October 19, November 1 and November 29, 2021, Nikol Pashinyan transferred 972 records of minefields located in Artsakh to Azerbaijan without preconditions. In January 2024, he handed over eight additional minefield records to Baku. These maps were exceptionally important because, without them, clearing the mined areas would have required 10-15 years. This list of concessions does not include the consequences of the 44-day war, as a result of which we lost our victory and the second Armenian statehood, Artsakh, with its 12,000 square kilometers of territory, millennia-old historical and cultural heritage, monuments, mines and all its wealth. These are the major concessions made unilaterally under written or verbal agreements with Aliyev. However, Baku’s demands do not end there. Azerbaijan is effectively demanding the dissolution of the Minsk Group, amendments to Armenia’s Constitution, the provision of a ‘corridor’ (which, of course, they will call the provision of a road), the settlement of Azerbaijanis in Armenia, and the handover of ‘enclaves’. Consequently, the capitulator has exhausted every attempt to falsify facts, lie, distort reality and conceal his destructive role in the fate of the nation,” the post reads. On October 7, during the government’s question-and-answer session in parliament, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, responding to a question from Deputy Speaker Aram Vardevanyan, stated that the Armenian side had made no concessions whatsoever. “Tell me, what have we conceded? Have you answered this question?” he said.

Don’t sign up for Starlink.’ Photograph: Matt Rourke/AP Opinion Elon Musk Defund Elon Musk Robert Reich No private individual should have the power to determine US foreign policy, as Musk has attempted to do in Ukraine Tue 27 Oct 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 06.02 EDT Share H e’s Exhibit A on why billionaire wealth should be taxed, why we must get big money out of politics, why billionaires shouldn’t be allowed to buy up major media, and why our government shouldn’t give them huge military contracts. I’m talking about Elon Musk , of course. According to the Wall Street Journal , Musk “ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink relied on by Ukraine”. The decision “sparked panic in Kyiv and confusion inside the Trump administration, U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter said”. Musk and Trump, the Journal noted, have both “expressed anger at Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries in recent weeks, which the president blames for high energy prices” – although the high prices are really due to Trump’s war in Iran. This month, Musk slowed “the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network … rendering some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless”. According to the Journal, “Musk and Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call soon after the slowdown became public.” Who gave Musk authority to slow his satellite service in the first place? Musk finally admitted this weekend that he had pulled the plug because, he wrote on Twitter/X : “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people.” So Musk can decide on his own when a foreign country working alongside the United States against a brutal dictator can have access to vital US intelligence? Every time I list another of Musk’s outrages, someone says: “Yes, but he’s an innovator!” He’s not. As is made clear in Alex Gibney’s smart new documentary, Musk , Elon didn’t invent Tesla . He didn’t invent X. He got plenty of help founding SpaceX . Musk is to innovation what Trump is to governing. We must tax the wealth of billionaires, not just income. California can lead the way | Ro Khanna Read more Both are conmen. Both are megalomaniacs. Both love authoritarians and detest democracy. Neither believes in (or harbors an ounce of) empathy toward anyone. Both think nothing of corrupting governments for personal gain. Both spout bigoted filth all hours of the day and night to hundreds of millions of people. OK, let me just say it out loud: Both Musk and Trump are loathsome human beings. Someday historians will come up with an explanation of how two such awful people could have become the two most powerful people in the US, if not the world (what was it about the US in the early 21st century?). But for now, the goal of all sane people must be to defund both and get them as far away from politics as possible. That will be difficult, to be sure. Musk has so far sunk roughly $445m into the 2026 midterm election cycle – all to help Republicans retain control of Congress. That makes him the largest single known donor in the entire midterm elections. Will he expect a return on his investment? skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly, for twelve weeks Sign up to How We Win Bernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk. after newsletter promotion Hell, he spent a quarter of a billion dollars in 2024 to help Trump win re-election and ended up with access to vast troves of government data, along with billions of dollars’ worth of no-bid contracts with the Pentagon. His Starlink satellite system is now key to the military strategy of the United States as well as that of Ukraine. He was also rewarded with a chainsaw inaptly named “department of government efficiency”, which he used to destroy USAID and slash other government agencies he doesn’t like. Musk has given at least $168m to Texas Super Pacs seeking to elect Republican Ken Paxton to the Senate, despite (or is it because of?) Paxton’s long record of ethical lapses and legal controversies. Musk’s businesses are headquartered in Texas, so he needs friends there. Musk recently pushed the false story to his 242 million followers on X that James Talarico, Paxton’s Democratic opponent, was absent from the campaign trail because he had suffered a mental breakdown and was receiving counseling at the Lindner Center of Hope, a mental health center in Ohio. In the battle of Elon Musk v the press, we can’t let truth be the loser | Jane Martinson Read more That story has been thoroughly debunked. Security camera footage shows Talarico at home, not at an Ohio mental health facility. (Meanwhile, according to the Wall Street Journal , on New Year’s Eve 2024, Paxton partied in Dubai with his extramarital girlfriend and two fugitives from charges of about $300m in healthcare fraud in the US. One of the men donated $190,000 to Paxton, $25,000 of it after he was indicted.) The project of defunding Musk will probably have to wait until after 20 January 2029, when, let’s pray, we have a sane administration in Washington that will end all government contracts with him (his support for rightwing extremists around the world makes him a security risk), bust up his monopolies (a reinvigorated Federal Trade Commission and Federal Communications Commission will see to it), and impose a significant wealth tax on him. No private individual should have the power to determine US foreign policy, as Musk has attempted to do in Ukraine. If Musk’s Starlink system has become so central to military strategy that its Pentagon contracts can’t be cancelled, it should be nationalized. (After I suggested this on my podcast last Saturday, Musk posted: “Stealing companies is a serious crime. Prison for Reich.” But you don’t have to wait until Musk is officially defunded. Stop buying Teslas. Don’t use X. Don’t sign up for Starlink. And support politicians who promise to defund him. Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com .
